strong.text: You held tetralogy of Fallot together as one story: a malaligned septum, a blocked outflow, and consequences that follow from them. Your answers were mostly right the first time, so the review cards below are for spacing, not repair. Do them on the days shown, then test yourself on the PYQ-versus-current-source pairs, since those are where a well-built model still loses marks.

mixed.text: Parts of tetralogy of Fallot are solid and parts are still a list. Read the objective notes below: the secure ones need only the review cards, the shaky and gap ones need the mechanism rebuilt. Start with whichever is marked 'you were sure', because a confident error corrected now sticks better than almost anything else. Then redo the spell and anatomy chains from the outflow obstruction.

weak.text: Several core parts of tetralogy of Fallot are still memorised rather than derived, and that is useful information, not a verdict. Do not start from the cards. Redraw the heart from one anteriorly malaligned septum, trace the blood from the blocked outflow, and only then move to spells and surgery. Take the gap objectives below in order, then use the review cards on their schedule.

secure.text: You separate the four components of TOF from lesions that merely accompany it, and you know the fifth that makes the pentalogy. Keep deriving them from the malaligned septum rather than reciting them.

shaky.text: The four components and the pentalogy are mostly there but not yet reliable. Redraw them: large malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular obstruction, RVH. ASD and PDA may accompany TOF, and TOF plus ASD is the old pentalogy. Redo the 'which is NOT' cards.

gap.text: The tetrad is still a loose list for you, so shunts and hypertrophy slip in. Rebuild it from one anteriorly malaligned VSD: the aorta overrides, the infundibulum narrows, the RV thickens. ASD and PDA only accompany. Review the component and pentalogy cards first.

secure.text: You trace the chain in the right order: infundibular obstruction, blood bypassing the lungs, then RVH as the consequence. That chain lets you predict the ECG and film instead of memorising them.

shaky.text: The chain from outflow obstruction to secondary RVH holds in places. Say it aloud from the start: infundibular narrowing, pressure load on the RV, RVH, and flow shunted toward the aorta. Practise predicting before you read the options.

gap.text: The causal chain is the weak point: RVH may be sitting at the start instead of the end. Trace it step by step: infundibular obstruction, RV pressure load, then hypertrophy, with blood bypassing the lungs. Review the mechanism card before any other.

secure.text: You read cyanosis in TOF as a balance between RVOT and systemic resistance, and you keep 'most common cyanotic CHD' apart from 'usually presents as a cyanotic neonate'. That is the qualifier habit the exam rewards.

shaky.text: Cyanosis as a balance of RVOT against systemic resistance is partly in place. Restate the rule: if RVOT resistance is below systemic resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic, a pink Tet. Re-read superlative stems for qualifiers before answering.

gap.text: You may still read TOF as always blue from birth, or merge 'most common' with 'presents as'. Learn the rule: RVOT resistance below systemic resistance gives a pink Tet. Then contrast the unqualified 'most common' stem with presentation age. Review those two cards first.

secure.text: Your auscultation picture fits TOF: harsh ejection murmur, inaudible P2, and a murmur that softens in a spell because less blood crosses the outflow.

shaky.text: The TOF auscultation picture is partly there. Anchor three points: a harsh ejection murmur at the left sternal border, an inaudible P2, and a murmur that gets softer, not louder, in a spell. Ask how much blood is crossing the RVOT.

gap.text: Auscultation is a gap. 'More obstruction, louder murmur' holds at baseline but fails in a spell, when the murmur softens. Also expect an inaudible P2, not a loud one. Review the spell murmur card and the P2 card, asking each time how much blood reaches the pulmonary valve.

secure.text: You predict the ECG and film from right ventricular load: right axis deviation, RVH, oligaemic lungs, and a boot shape that is classic but not guaranteed. This is derivation, not recall.

shaky.text: The ECG and film are partly derived and partly recalled. Rebuild both from the RV: right axis and tall R in V1, an upturned apex from RVH, oligaemic lungs because blood bypasses them. The boot shape is a 'may classically' sign.

gap.text: The ECG and chest film are not yet tied to the right ventricle. Derive them: RV pressure load gives right axis deviation and RVH, the apex turns up, and lungs look oligaemic. The boot shape is classic, not always present. Review the ECG and X-ray cards first.

secure.text: You name echocardiography as the diagnostic gold standard and give CT and MRI their separate jobs. You ranked tests by the question asked, which is the right habit.

shaky.text: Echo as the gold standard is mostly secure, but the roles of CT and MRI are blurred. Match each to one job: echo diagnoses, CT shows complex morphology, MRI gives anatomy and function without radiation. Redo the test-ladder card.

gap.text: Test selection is a gap: you may be ranking tests by invasiveness or detail. Ask 'diagnose, or plan surgery?' Echo is the gold standard for diagnosis; CT shows morphology; MRI adds function without radiation. Review the investigation ladder card first.

secure.text: You order tet-spell management correctly, bedside first, and you name what each step pulls: knee-chest raises systemic resistance, oxygen dilates the pulmonary bed, fluids fill the RV.

shaky.text: Spell management is partly secure. Rehearse the order and the lever together: knee-chest raises systemic resistance, oxygen dilates the pulmonary bed, fluids improve RV filling, beta-blockers slow the rate, phenylephrine raises afterload, morphine sedates. Redo the ordering card.

gap.text: Spell management is a gap, and it is the highest-yield area. Start bedside: knee-chest to raise systemic resistance, then oxygen. Then fluids for RV filling, then beta-blocker or phenylephrine. Do not treat it like heart failure. Review the ordering and lever cards before anything else.

secure.text: You time repair by the infant in front of you and know the Blalock-Taussig shunt joins subclavian artery to the ipsilateral pulmonary artery. Both come from qualifiers, not one fixed timeline.

shaky.text: Repair timing and the BT shunt are partly secure. Anchor: StatPearls defers complete repair to after the first 3 months, timing is still debated, and the BT shunt joins subclavian artery to ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery. Check symptoms before timing.

gap.text: Surgical timing and the shunt are a gap. Avoid one timeline for all infants: StatPearls describes deferring complete repair to after 3 months, and the debate continues. The BT shunt joins subclavian artery to ipsilateral pulmonary artery. Review the timing and shunt cards.

secure.text: You know the repair leaves its own legacy: pulmonary regurgitation from RVOT reconstruction, the commonest reason for reoperation, plus lifelong arrhythmia, sudden-death and endocarditis risk.

shaky.text: The after-repair picture is partly secure. Hold two ideas: reconstruction of the RVOT causes pulmonary regurgitation, the commonest reoperation indication, and repaired TOF still carries ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death and endocarditis risk. Redo the after-repair cards.

gap.text: The after-repair picture is a gap. Repair is not a cure: reconstructing the RVOT causes pulmonary regurgitation, the most common reoperation indication, and arrhythmia, sudden death and endocarditis risks persist. Ask what the operation changed, not which defect returns. Review those cards first.

secure.text: You rank the causes of death in unrepaired TOF correctly, with hypoxic spells first, the event this module drilled.

shaky.text: The ranking of deaths in unrepaired TOF is partly there. Anchor it: hypoxic spells about two-thirds (68%), cerebrovascular accidents 17%, brain abscesses 13%. Frequency beats vividness.

gap.text: The ranking of deaths in unrepaired TOF slipped. Without surgery hypoxic spells cause 68%, strokes 17% and brain abscesses 13%. The vivid complication is not the commonest. Review the ranking card, anchored to the spells you drilled.

secure.text: You hold the associations and figures with an anchor, including where sources disagree. This is a non-core area, so this is a bonus.

shaky.text: The associations and figures are partly there. Anchor them: right aortic arch in 20-25%, 22q11.2 deletion the commonest syndromic association with sources giving up to 15% versus 6%, and incidence quoted differently by different sources. Low priority.

gap.text: Associations and figures slipped, but this is non-core, so protect your time. Anchor three things: right aortic arch 20-25%, 22q11.2 deletion as the main syndromic link, and the fact that sources quote different shares and incidences. Do these cards last.

secure.text: You can give both the PYQ key and the current source where they diverge. That double answer is exactly what lets you score on the exam and still know the truth.

shaky.text: You sometimes see where a PYQ key and the current source diverge. Practise saying both: PYQs keyed ASD, PDA and LVH as not part of TOF; boot shape is a classic sign that many infants may not show; 'most common' carries an age qualifier.

gap.text: The PYQ-versus-current-source divergences did not land, though this is non-core. For each pair, learn the exam key first, then the qualifier: the age in 'most common cyanotic CHD', the 'may classically' wording on the boot shape, and the four components in current sources.

avoided.text: You kept the tetrad as one malformation, not a list of shunts. Keep deriving it.

fell_recovered.text: You first added a familiar shunt to the four, then rebuilt them from the malaligned septum. Under exam pressure the 'which is NOT' wording can pull ASD, PDA or LVH back in, so derive the four again each time.

fell_open.text: You are storing TOF as a list of familiar shunts and hypertrophies, so ASD, PDA or LVH slip in. Redraw it from one malaligned VSD: aorta overrides, infundibulum narrows, RV thickens. Then redo the 'which is NOT' cards. PYQs keyed ASD, PDA and LVH as not part of TOF.

avoided.text: You knew the obstruction is infundibular and RVH follows from it.

fell_recovered.text: You first reversed cause and effect, then traced the chain. A rushed stem can make the thick RV look primary again, so begin at the outflow obstruction each time.

fell_open.text: You are treating the obstruction as a simple valve stenosis and the thick RV as a primary defect. The order is reversed: infundibular obstruction loads the RV, and RVH is secondary to that pressure. Trace septum, infundibulum, pressure load, hypertrophy, then redo the mechanism card.

avoided.text: You knew pentalogy is TOF plus an ASD.

fell_recovered.text: You first swapped in another lesion for the fifth component, then fixed it. Familiar shunts blur together under time pressure, so tie the pentalogy to ASD.

fell_open.text: You are treating ASD and PDA as interchangeable extra shunts, so the fifth member is a guess. Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus an atrial septal defect, an old term seldom used now. PDA may accompany TOF but is not the fifth. Redo the pentalogy card.

avoided.text: You treated the boot shape as a classic sign with an RV cause, not a must-have.

fell_recovered.text: You first stretched 'classic' into 'always' or blamed the wrong chamber, then corrected it. The superlative creeps back in recall, so read the qualifier and name the RV.

fell_open.text: You have turned 'boot-shaped heart' into an always-present sign, or credited the left side or a big pulmonary artery. The upturned apex comes from RVH with a concave pulmonary segment, and the film may classically show it. Review the X-ray card and name the chamber every time.

avoided.text: You paired the boot-shaped, oligaemic film with TOF.

fell_recovered.text: You first mixed up the cyanotic heart disease signs, then anchored the TOF film to its mechanism. Under pressure a list of famous signs can blur, so rebuild from the RV.

fell_open.text: You are matching radiograph signs from a memorised list rather than from mechanism. Build the TOF film from RVH and low pulmonary flow: upturned apex, concave pulmonary segment, oligaemic lungs, normal-sized heart. Redo the X-ray description card.

avoided.text: You read the qualifier before answering 'most common'.

fell_recovered.text: You first dropped the age qualifier, then separated 'most common' from 'presents as'. Superlative stems are where that comes back, so underline the age group.

fell_open.text: You are answering 'most common cyanotic CHD' without its qualifier and merging it with 'usually presents as a cyanotic neonate'. Unqualified, the key is TOF; PYQs add 'beyond the neonatal period'. Redo the qualifier card, underlining the age group.

avoided.text: You knew cyanosis depends on RVOT against systemic resistance, so the pink Tet did not surprise you.

fell_recovered.text: You first assumed every TOF is blue from birth, then met the pink Tet. Under exam pressure 'cyanotic heart disease' will tempt you to say blue, so recall the resistance balance.

fell_open.text: You are equating 'cyanotic heart disease' with 'blue at birth'. If RVOT resistance is below systemic resistance the child is minimally cyanotic, a pink Tet with a loud murmur. Redo the pink Tet card and say the resistance rule aloud.

avoided.text: You knew the murmur softens in a spell.

fell_recovered.text: You first expected a louder murmur, then traced the falling flow. 'Worse stenosis, louder murmur' is a strong habit, so ask how much blood crosses the RVOT.

fell_open.text: You applied the static rule 'more obstruction, louder murmur' to a spell. In a spell blood bypasses the lungs, so less crosses the outflow and the murmur softens. A quiet murmur in a blue, crying child is worse, not better. Review the spell murmur card.

avoided.text: You knew knee-chest works through systemic resistance.

fell_recovered.text: You first put the lever on the pulmonary side, then rebuilt the balance. Knee-chest and oxygen sit together in memory, so ask which side each one pushes.

fell_open.text: You are placing knee-chest on the pulmonary side. It raises systemic vascular resistance, which pushes blood towards the lungs; oxygen is the one that dilates the pulmonary bed. Pair knee-chest with phenylephrine, not oxygen. Redo the lever card.

avoided.text: You started the spell with position and oxygen.

fell_recovered.text: You first reached for a drug, then put the bedside steps first. The active-sounding drug is tempting in a crisis, so rehearse the order.

fell_open.text: You know the spell treatments but not the order, and reach for the most active drug or airway step first. Start with knee-chest and oxygen, then IV fluids, then beta-blocker or phenylephrine, with morphine as sedative. Redo the ordering card until it is automatic.

avoided.text: You treated the spell by filling the RV and raising afterload.

fell_recovered.text: You first reached for heart-failure measures, then traced RV filling. Heart-failure reflexes return fast, so ask what each drug does to filling and systemic resistance.

fell_open.text: You are treating a spell like heart failure, with diuretics, fluid restriction or afterload lowering. A spell needs RV filling and higher systemic resistance: fluids fill the RV, beta-blockers aid filling, phenylephrine raises afterload. Redo the which-is-NOT and fluid cards.

avoided.text: You named echo as the diagnostic gold standard.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked a more invasive test, then placed each on the ladder. Detail looks like authority under pressure, so ask 'diagnose or plan surgery?'

fell_open.text: You are ranking tests by invasiveness or detail. Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosing TOF; catheterisation and CT are not. Ask what question the test answers. Revisit the investigation ladder card.

avoided.text: You matched each imaging test to its job.

fell_recovered.text: You first treated the tests as interchangeable, then matched each to a job. Echo, CT and MRI blur under pressure, so tie each to one question.

fell_open.text: You are treating echo, CT and MRI as interchangeable. Echo diagnoses, contrast-enhanced CT shows complex morphology, MRI gives anatomy and function without ionising radiation. Low yield, so revisit the pairing card once.

avoided.text: You kept the TOF ECG and film right-sided and oligaemic.

fell_recovered.text: You first put the changes on the left, then derived them from the RV load. A stored word like 'hypertrophy' loses its side under pressure, so derive it each time.

fell_open.text: You are storing 'hypertrophy' without a side and expecting a VSD to flood the lungs. TOF loads the RV: right axis deviation, RVH, and oligaemic lungs because blood bypasses them. Derive each film and ECG from the RV, then redo the ECG card.

avoided.text: You expected an inaudible P2 in TOF.

fell_recovered.text: You first borrowed a loud or split P2, then linked it to low flow. The word 'pulmonary' pulls a loud P2 back, so ask how much blood reaches the valve.

fell_open.text: You are importing a loud P2 from other conditions. In TOF the pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible, because little blood reaches the pulmonary valve. Ask what flow reaches the valve. Revisit the auscultation card.

avoided.text: You paired TOF with 22q11.2 deletion and kept its share modest.

fell_recovered.text: You first reached for Down syndrome or an inflated share, then corrected it. Famous syndromes come to mind first, so anchor TOF to 22q11.2.

fell_open.text: You are matching syndromes by fame, or stretching 'most common association' into 'most cases'. 22q11.2 deletion is the commonest syndromic association, with sources giving up to 15% versus 6% in one cohort. Re-do the association card and the share card.

avoided.text: Your TOF numbers were anchored.

fell_recovered.text: You first swapped figures, then anchored them. Digits blur quickly, so use anchors rather than memory.

fell_open.text: You are holding the figures without an anchor. A right aortic arch occurs in 20-25%, about one in four or five; incidence is quoted differently by sources. This is low yield, so spend one pass on the numbers card, not more.

avoided.text: You timed repair by the infant's features.

fell_recovered.text: You first used one timeline for every infant, then used the qualifiers. A single timeline is tempting in recall, so ask 'symptomatic? high-risk?'

fell_open.text: You are applying one repair timeline to every infant. StatPearls describes deferring complete repair until after 3 months, and the timing is still debated. Qualifiers decide it. Review the timing card, asking about symptoms first.

avoided.text: You knew the BT shunt joins subclavian to pulmonary artery.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked another connection or treated the shunt as the repair, then fixed it. Eponymous shunts blur, so anchor the BT connection.

fell_open.text: You have the eponymous shunts in one pile. The Blalock-Taussig shunt joins the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery. It is not a definitive repair. Anchor that one pair before others. Revisit the shunt card.

avoided.text: You knew pulmonary regurgitation is the repair's own legacy.

fell_recovered.text: You first expected the old defects to return, then traced the RVOT reconstruction. Intuition favours residual defects, so ask what the operation changed.

fell_open.text: You expect the original defects to return, not the problem the operation creates. Reconstruction of the RVOT causes pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary insufficiency is the most common reoperation indication. Review the after-repair card.

avoided.text: You knew repaired TOF carries lifelong risks.

fell_recovered.text: You first treated repair as cure, then met the arrhythmia and endocarditis risks. 'Repaired' sounds finished, so keep the lifelong qualifier.

fell_open.text: You are equating repair with cure. Ventricular arrhythmias occur in 40-50% of repaired adults, sudden death risk is 6-9% at 30 years, and endocarditis risk is present repaired or unrepaired. Review the follow-up card.

avoided.text: You knew hypoxic spells are the leading cause of death in unrepaired TOF.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked the vivid complication, then anchored to the 68%. Brain abscess is memorable, so anchor spells at about two-thirds.

fell_open.text: You let a vivid complication override frequency. Without surgery hypoxic spells cause 68% of deaths, strokes 17% and brain abscesses 13%. Anchor spells at two-thirds. Low yield, so a single pass on the ranking card is enough.

E1.text: You sometimes carry a sign across from a different lesion, such as a loud P2. Next time ask which finding discriminates this lesion, and what flow produces it.

E2.text: You tend to add familiar items to a fixed list. When a set is defined, rebuild it from its logic, here the malaligned septum, instead of recalling names. Then run 'which is NOT' questions.

E3.text: Your mechanism errors share a pattern: a lever or direction is reversed. Before choosing, predict the direction from the physiology, here the RVOT versus systemic resistance balance, then compare with the options.

E4.text: You tend to stretch a 'may classically' or 'usually' statement into 'always'. Read the qualifier in every stem and ask for one counter-case before committing.

E6.text: Your errors cluster on numbers and rankings held without an anchor. Tie each figure to something meaningful, and re-test it in another form.

E7.text: You tend to drop the qualifier that makes a statement true, such as age, repaired or unrepaired, or symptomatic. Underline the qualifier in each stem first.

E8.text: You rank tests by detail or invasiveness rather than by the question asked. Before choosing, ask whether the aim is to diagnose, to show morphology, or to measure function.

E9.text: You know the treatments but not their order. Rehearse sequences aloud with a reason for each step, bedside measures first, drugs after.

E10.text: You tend to match items by familiarity from an undifferentiated pile. Pair each item with its single anchor, and test the pair in both directions.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. That is where the learning is: these are the ones you will remember best once corrected. Before your next 'Sure', name the finding that proves it. Review the cards for your confident errors first.

underconfident.text: You tapped Guessing on several answers you got right. Your knowledge is ahead of your confidence. Commit when you can state the mechanism behind an answer, and use Guessing only when you cannot. Practice with cards will close this.

calibrated.text: Your Sure and Guessing taps matched your results well. That calibration lets you spend revision time where your knowledge is thin, instead of where it feels thin.

hints_heavy.text: You opened hints three or more times. Used well that is a strategy, but the exam has no hints. For the objectives marked shaky or gap, retry the cards cold, without options visible, before opening the explanation.

hints_none.text: You did not open a hint, even after falling into a trap. Next time, when you feel unsure, use the hint to test your reasoning; it costs nothing and it reveals which part of the model is missing.

hinted_only.text: On some objectives you were right only after a hint. That counts as progress, but it is not yet unaided recall. Redo those cards without hints, and treat any miss as the place to study.

fast_lane.text: You answered the diagnostic probes correctly and with confidence, so you skipped some worked explanations. That is the right use of the fast lane. The cards still matter, so do them on the schedule shown.

gap.text: Take the gap objectives in order, starting with any marked 'you were sure'. For each, read the repair in the matching review card, then redraw the chain on paper from memory. Return to the card on days 1 and 3, then continue the schedule.

clear.text: No gaps showed up. Do the review cards on the days shown, starting with any shaky objectives or traps you fell into. Then practise PYQ-style stems cold, without hints, since cold performance is what the exam tests.
